name: Yora
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.quote: I have not done a study of Yora stress. Where grammatical tone is discussed, some of the nouns are marked for tone. On two-syllable nouns marked for tone, an accent mark over a vowel indicates high tone and no accent mark on the other vowel indicates low tone. See section 2.3 for examples having grammatical tone marking. (p. 16) High tone or stress may play a part also, since the high tone o's in noko at the beginning of a sentence have been pronounced [u] but the low tone o's in noko in a different environment have been pronounced [o]. (p. 15)
new_statements.citation: Lord, Mary Ann. 2016. Some Features of Yora Grammar. Documento de Trabajo 33. Lima: Instituto Lingüístico de Verano.

new_statements.rule_in_words: No stress-placement rule is given: the only grammar of Yora states explicitly that stress was not studied. What the source does describe is grammatical tone: on one noun class, ergative case is marked by a high-low tone pattern plus nasalization (e.g. absolutive áfá 'his mother' with level tone vs ergative ã́fã), and the author marks high tone with an acute accent on two-syllable nouns where relevant (§2.3, pp. 29-31).
new_statements.exceptions: None (no rule stated). The author notes tone marking is applied only where grammatical tone is under discussion and does not imply the rest of the word or sentence is tone-marked (p. 16).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level remarks on two-syllable nouns (case-marking tone); the p. 15 remark concerns sentence-initial vs other position of noko. Data are from speakers of Santa Rosa del Serjali (upper Mishagua), selected to minimise Yaminahua/Sharanahua influence (§1.1.7).
new_statements.first_reading: tone language with a stress statement
new_statements.identity_note: Lord 2016 describes the Yora of Santa Rosa del Serjali and San Martín on the upper Mishagua River (Ucayali, Peru), self-designation Yora [yuɾɐ] 'people', called 'Nahua' in Peruvian government records and 'Shara' locally; three claimed subgroups (Maxonafa, Roanifo, Iskonafa) with no detectable dialect split. Fleck 2013 (p. 86) treats modern Yora as 'Parkenawa', a dialect of Yaminawa (yami1256), and reserves 'Yura' for a historical group name; Peru's MINEDU classification (cited by Lord) makes it closest to Yaminahua. Lord's data were chosen to minimise Yaminahua (Purús/Piedras dialect) and Sharanahua influence.

sources.note: §1.2.2 'Alphabet and pronunciation guide' (pp. 13-17) is a pronunciation guide, not a phonology; p. 16: 'I have not done a study of Yora stress.' sources.note: Family-level only: 'Stress assignment often depends on the syllable structure of the word, but details vary from language to language. In Capanawa, Shipibo, Canamari and some others of the Capanawa subgroup, a closed second syllable is stressed.' Yoranawa appears only in the language table (200 speakers, Peru) and in remarks on w/m/n allophony (Kim Fowler credited for Yoranawa data).

Bibliographic only: cites Fleck 2013 and Oliveira 2023 for subclassification; links PHOIBLE, Grambank, OLAC. Three of the four Glottolog 5.1 descriptive refs in WORLD_TARGETS (Lewandowska-Tomaszczyk 1995; Barrajón López 2023; Bhatia, Teng & Allen 2018) are misattributed to this language and are not about Yora at all.

sources.citation: Fleck, David W. 2013. Panoan Languages and Linguistics. Anthropological Papers of the American Museum of Natural History 99: 1-112. doi:10.5531/sp.anth.0099
sources.note: Family-level phonology overview (pp. 43-44) says nothing about stress and lists contrastive tone only for Chakobo, Kapanawa (Tapiche) and Amawaka; no Yora-specific statement. Classifies modern Yora as Parkenawa, a dialect of Yaminawa (p. 86 synonymy: 'Parkenawa (T1: II.C.viii.b, dialect of Yaminawa). syn: Nawa, Yora, Yura, Yoranahua'). Bibliography lists unpublished word lists (Faust 1984 'Parquenahua word list'; Lord 1996 'Word list: Sharanahua, Roadijo Yora, Yaminahua, Chitonahua'), ILV Yora literacy primers (1997a, 1997b, 2001, 2005) and an ELAR documentation deposit by C. Feather (p. 41).
